supports: Within-group information coverage was randomized across meeting groups at 0%, 50% and 80%, and conditional on strata and subregion peers were random.
Being informed raised the application probability by 30 percentage points, having at least one informed group member by 29.1 points, and competition weakened diffusion by 21.2 points.
Diffusion was similar at 50% and 80% coverage, so adding informed members beyond the first did not raise the uninformed application probability much.
does_not_support: Treating this case as an adaptation of the paper's main question; the main intervention is a year of monthly meetings and the main outcome is revenue and profit.
Fitting an individual prediction equation from the three coefficients; the paper reports three separate regressions and does not combine them.
Adding the full-sample Info coefficient to the informed-group-member coefficient as if they came from the same population; that sum is an additivity assumption made by the project.
A zero baseline as the paper's control condition; 40% of control managers were also informed.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-11: a within-group information-coverage policy with competition moderating diffusion, expressed as a mixture of two complete information lists.

inspected: Abstract and Introduction (pp. 855-857): the predicted 0.053 gain for the bottom third and the negative observed effect, with students avoiding the intended peers
Section 2 (pp. 862-870): 20 control and 20 treatment squadrons, the integer program in equation (3), and the bimodal versus homogeneous squadron definitions on p. 865
Table IV (p. 868): predicted treatment effect of 0.053 for low predicted GPA students
Section 3 and Table VI (p. 871): -0.061 for low, 0.082 for middle, -0.012 for high ability, on 4,834 student-semester observations
Section 4 and Table VIII (p. 878): homophily in study partner and friend choice, 0.171 versus 0.125, and high SAT Verbal partners 3.9 percentage points lower
Section 5 (pp. 880-881): the paper states the exact cause cannot be known with certainty
not_inspected: The derivations of equations (1) and (2) in Section 1.2, the Supplemental Material tables, and full readings of Figures 1 to 5; no full-text verification claimed.

supports: A history-based resorting predicted a 0.053 grade-point gain for bottom-third students, while the experiment produced -0.061 for the same group.
Treated low-ability students formed more homogeneous subgroups and selected high SAT Verbal study partners less often, so being placed with a peer differs from interacting with that peer.
Middle-ability treated students gained 0.082, which the paper attributes to no longer interacting with low-ability students in homogeneous squadrons.
does_not_support: Treating this case as a reproduction of the paper's sorting policy; the paper reassigns students through an integer program, while the case keeps both groups fixed and assigns peer leaders.
Keeping the paper's random-assignment contrast; both lists act on already formed groups, so the case compares mild versus concentrated assignment.
Reading 0.053, -0.061 and 0.082 as individual treatment effects; 0.053 is a predicted group-level gain and the other two are coefficients on a treatment dummy.
Using one adjacency for every policy; the paper's network forms endogenously, and the case fixes adjacency so the mixture schema can express the policy.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-12: a fixed-adjacency leader-assignment policy whose outcome depends on the number of adjacent leaders, expressed as a mixture of two complete leader lists.

Section VI, equations (6)-(9) and Table 4 Panel B (pp. 2066-2070): sequential ordering on p. 2067, decay-adjusted effects 0.026, 0.037, 0.060, snowball shares 0, 30, 57 percent, and the note that fifth and later coworkers lack observations
Section VII (pp. 2071-2072): conclusions for policy design
not_inspected: The online Appendix construction of decay parameters, Figure A5, and the sample-restriction details of Section II; no full-text verification claimed.

supports: Fathers of children born after April 1, 1993 became eligible for paid leave, and take-up rose from 3 to 35 percent, a first stage of 32 percentage points.
Coworker effects rise with birth order inside a firm, from 0.026 to 0.037 to 0.060, with snowball shares of 0, 30 and 57 percent.
Brothers respond more strongly than coworkers, and earlier fathers influence later ones but not the reverse.
does_not_support: Treating 0.32 as a leave take-up level; the 35 percent figure is a post-reform participation rate, while the case uses only a change.
Adding 0.026, 0.037 and 0.060 across upstream fathers; they are reduced-form totals relative to the first covered coworker.
Treating the cutoff date as a schedulable policy instrument; the paper's date is set by the reform and supports an identification design, not a policy design.
Reading the eight fathers as the paper's sample or the case as a reproduction of equations (6)-(9); the structural betas are not reported.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-13: two complete start-date schedules drawn with equal probability, where a father's leave-probability change depends on his birth-order distance from the covered coworker in the same plant, expressed as a mixture of two schedules over one fixed adjacency.

source_cards.title: Learning about a New Technology: Pineapple in Ghana

inspected: Abstract (p. 35): farmers adjust inputs to align with surprisingly successful information neighbors
Introduction (pp. 35-38): the signed direction rule and the novice/veteran difference in the summary of findings
Section II (pp. 40-43): construction of M, its near-zero case, and the experience normalization
p. 51: the full signed definition of M
Table 4 note (p. 55): advice-question definition of information neighborhoods, sample of 107

Section IV text (pp. 56-58): one standard deviation of M (about four) for roughly four cedis per plant, no veteran response, insignificant financial neighbors, downward moves as real as upward ones, no own-plot versus neighbor-plot difference
Table 6 A (p. 59): M from own plots 1.46 (0.56) versus information neighbors 1.22 (0.31)
p. 60: no learning on the established maize-cassava mix
not_inspected: Appendix A, Table A1, and the construction details of the growing-conditions control; no full-text verification claimed.

supports: M is large and positive when a good-news experiment is much higher than the farmer's previous use, large and negative when much lower, and near zero when close (p. 51; p. 43).
Novices respond and veterans do not: 1.07 (0.22) versus -0.46 (0.34), different at the 3 percent level, with no evidence of veteran response in the text.
Strong partial correlations are driven as much by downward as by upward movement, and own-plot good news is not significantly different from neighbor-plot good news.
does_not_support: Reading the 1.05 coefficient as an exact multiplier; the text states about four for about four cedis, and the case rounds to 1.
Carrying the experience normalization of M into the case; only the sign implication is kept and the novice/veteran difference becomes two separate rules.

Treating demonstrations as the paper's experiments; experiments there are farmer-chosen and judged against growing conditions, while the case makes the demonstration level a lottery-set policy parameter.
Substituting geographic or financial neighbors for information neighbors; financial-neighbor coefficients are insignificant and geographic neighbors enter as a control.
Reading the eight farmers as the paper's sample: 107 cultivators, and the previous-use figures are project-built.
Extrapolating to established crops: the maize-cassava mix shows no learning.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-14: two complete demonstration arrangements drawn with equal probability over one fixed information network, where a novice's intensity change equals the demonstrated level minus previous use (zero when equal), veterans never move, and the demonstrator's own change counts; the target is the average signed change and can be negative.

source_cards.title: Identification of Endogenous Social Effects: The Reflection Problem

inspected: Abstract (p. 531): the reflection problem and the need for prior information on reference-group composition
Section 1 (pp. 531-532): the mirror metaphor and the theme of the paper
Section 2 opening (pp. 532-533): the linear model and the definitions of endogenous, exogenous and correlated effects; the high-school achievement example
p. 533: the tutoring example, the social multiplier with feedback, and exogenous/correlated effects not generating the multiplier
p. 534: the social equilibrium equation (3), its unique solution (4) provided beta differs from 1, and Proposition 1
p. 535: corollary to Proposition 1 and the nonlinear-model identification condition
p. 536: informed specification of reference groups as a necessary prelude
p. 537: the spatial autoregressive weighted-average form
p. 541: conclusions on tighter theory, richer data and experimental evidence
not_inspected: Sections 4-5 (dynamic models and consumer demand) and the proofs of the propositions; no full-text verification claimed.

supports: Individual outcomes vary with the reference-group average, and the group mean solves the social equilibrium equation (3) with unique solution (4) provided beta is not 1 (p. 533; p. 534).

An effective tutoring programme directly helps the tutored, indirectly helps all students as their achievement rises, with feedback to the tutored; exogenous and correlated effects do not generate this multiplier (p. 533).
Prior information specifying the composition of reference groups is a necessary prelude to analysis of social effects (Abstract p. 531; p. 536).
Endogenous effects cannot be distinguished from exogenous or correlated effects in observational data (Proposition 1, p. 534); the decomposition requires known rules or richer data (p. 541).
does_not_support: Reading beta=0.5 or the 4-point direct effect as the paper's numbers: the paper reports no numbers, the parameters are project-built and constrained only by beta not equal to 1 (p. 534).
Treating the case as a demonstration of the paper's identification result: the case is a policy computation with fully known rules, not inference from data.
Treating the lottery as the paper's design: tutoring there is a hypothetical example without quotas or randomization (p. 533).
Adding contextual or correlated effects: the case keeps only the endogenous effect as in the paper's restricted model (p. 535).
Reading the six students as any sample: the paper has no data and the roster is project-built.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-15: two complete tutoring arrangements drawn with equal probability over two classes with within-class reference groups; a tutored student gains 4 points directly and every student gains 0.5 points per point of the final class-mean gain, so the answer solves the social-equilibrium equation on each class; the target is the average gain over the six students and the changed-target variant evaluates one student only.

source_cards.title: Confidence Intervals for Partially Identified Parameters
source_cards.article_type: Journal research article (Notes and Comments; identification and inference theory)

inspected: Abstract and Section 1 (p. 1845): partially identified parameters and the confidence-interval question
Section 2 (p. 1846): the abstract structure, Lemma 1, and the substantive choice between covering the true value and covering the region
Section 3 (pp. 1847-1849): the missing-data example with known p, the identification region [mu*p, mu*p+(1-p)], the point-identified case p=1, and the three intervals
Section 4 (pp. 1849-1850): the general case, Assumption 1, equations (6)-(7), Lemma 4
Appendix (pp. 1851-1857): proofs located; Lemmas 5-10 not re-derived
not_inspected: Step-by-step re-derivation of the proofs of Lemmas 5-10; formula-level subscripts in the extracted text are damaged and formulas are cited by equation number.

supports: The abstract structure of partially identified parameters and the substantive choice between intervals covering the true value and intervals covering the region (Section 2, p. 1846).

With a bounded outcome, some data missing and known p, the population mean is theta = mu*p + lambda*(1-p) with lambda in [0,1], and the identification region is [mu*p, mu*p + (1-p)] of width 1-p (Section 3, p. 1847).
In the point-identified case p = 1 the region collapses to the point mu (p. 1847).
The mean of the observed subpopulation, mu, is point identified while the population mean theta is only set-identified; the contrast drives the three-interval comparison (pp. 1847-1849).
does_not_support: Reading [1/6, 5/6] or [1/2, 1/2] as the paper's numbers: the paper reports no empirical values; all case numbers are project-built.

Reading the chain network, the quota-2 pilot or the known/missing split as the paper's design: the paper has no network and no quota; missingness there is stochastic with a known propensity score, while the case's missingness is structural (zero-probability cells under the pilot law).

Borrowing the confidence-interval machinery (three intervals, the C_N equation, Lemmas 1-10) into the deterministic finite model: the case uses only the Section 3 identification-region structure and the point-identification limit.
Treating the two known endpoints as any sample: the roster, the means and the bounds are project-built declarations.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-16: six teams on a chain, a quota-2 pilot that reveals the full-exposure cell only for the two endpoints (mu=1/2, mass p=1/3), interior teams' full-exposure means only bounded in [0,1]; the original target reproduces [mu*p, mu*p+(1-p)] = [1/6, 5/6] as a PARTIAL interval, the changed-target variant evaluates the two revealed endpoints and collapses to the point 1/2, and the missing-condition variant drops the complete-model declaration.

source_cards.title: Estimation and Confidence Regions for Parameter Sets in Econometric Models
source_cards.article_type: Journal research article (identification and inference theory)

inspected: Abstract and Section 1 (pp. 1243-1246): criterion-function framework, identified set as the set of minimizers, moment inequalities and equalities
Section 2.1 (pp. 1246-1247): Theta_I = {theta : Q(theta) = 0}, moment inequalities (2.1), the half-space/polyhedron statement, moment equalities (2.4)-(2.6)
Section 2.2 (p. 1248): Example 1 interval data, its moment function and Theta_I = {theta : E[Y1] <= theta <= E[Y2]}; Examples 2-4 located
Section 2.3 (pp. 1250-1252): contour sets, the inferential statistic C_n in (2.9), rates and the degeneracy property
Sections 3.3-3.5 (pp. 1256-1259) and the conclusion (p. 1270): confidence regions, subsampling, asymptotics located but not used
not_inspected: Step-by-step re-derivation of Section 4 (conditions verified for moment-condition models) and Section 5 (regions for a point in Theta_I); formula-level subscripts in the extracted text are damaged and formulas are cited by equation number.

supports: The identified set as the zero set of a nonnegative population criterion, Theta_I = {theta in Theta : Q(theta) = 0}, generally multivalued (Section 2, p. 1246).
Moment-inequality restrictions E_P[m_i(theta)] <= 0 and, with linear moment functions, Theta_I as an intersection of linear half-spaces that may be a triangle, a trapezoid or a polyhedron (p. 1246).
Moment-equality restrictions and the GMM form of the criterion (p. 1247, equations (2.4)-(2.6)).
Example 1: interval data with Theta_I = {theta : E[Y1] <= theta <= E[Y2]} and a two-kink criterion (p. 1248).
Contour sets C_n(c) of the sample criterion as the general form of estimators and regions (p. 1250; equation (3.2) on p. 1253).
does_not_support: Reading [7/12, 3/4] or [1/2, 3/4] as the paper's numbers: the paper reports no empirical values; all case numbers are project-built.
Reading the chain network, the quota-2 pilot, the archive bounds or the equality/bracket split as the paper's design: the paper has no network and no quota.

Borrowing the estimation and inference machinery (the choice of c-hat, subsampling on p. 1257, asymptotics of C_n on p. 1259, Hausdorff rates and the degeneracy property on pp. 1251 and 1254) into the deterministic finite model.
Treating Theta_I as sharp by definition: the paper defines Theta_I by the model's restrictions and does not assert sharpness; sharpness here is checked by replaying the project certificate.
Reading Example 1's Y1, Y2 as the case's [1/2, 3/4]: the paper brackets realizations, the case declares per-node mean brackets.
source_cards.project_use: Scenario adaptation for LIT-NET-17: six stores on a chain, a quota-2 pilot that reveals the full-exposure cell only for the two endpoints (3/4, equality constraints), interior stores' full-exposure means only known to lie in the archive interval [1/2, 3/4] (two inequality constraints each); the original target gives the PARTIAL interval [7/12, 3/4] of width 1/6, the changed target evaluates only the four archive-covered stores and collapses to the archive interval itself [1/2, 3/4] with informative=false, and the missing-condition variant drops the complete-model declaration and returns NEEDS_INPUT.

evidence_rules: Literature metadata or an abstract is not evidence of a fully checked theorem.
A project-derived theorem must be labeled as such and linked to its complete derivation.
A literature card cannot replace independent scientific approval, target binding, or executable replay.
A path to a test is not a claim that the test passed; read the dated result report.
This catalog covers selected finite mean-box, contrast, mean-order and DAG adjustment research; not all Identification literature.
